factsAccepted: Net margin declined from 10% ($1.5M profit on $15M revenue) to 6% ($900k profit), a 40% decline in profitability. Revenue growing 12% YoY indicates volume is not the problem; margin compression is the issue.
Cost per visit trending up. Patient visit revenue averaging $180, but operating cost per visit trending up due to labor cost increases and overhead allocation across growing patient base.

Insurance mix is shifting toward lower-paying plans. Over the two-year window in which net margin fell from 10% to 6%, the share of visits reimbursed by higher-paying commercial plans declined while government and narrow-network plan share rose, pulling blended realized revenue per visit down even though list charges and the ~$180 average visit revenue figure are roughly flat. With volumes up 8% YoY, total reimbursement still grows but per-visit reimbursement is eroding.

Clinical labor is the dominant and rising cost driver. Physician and clinical staff compensation must be held flat-to-up to retain providers in a tight recruiting market, and these costs are spread across 8 locations and 120 employees. As the clinic scaled patient volume, fixed and semi-fixed staffing was added ahead of fully utilized demand at newer sites, raising cost per visit faster than the modest growth in revenue per visit.

There is no service-line or per-location profitability reporting, so the clinic cannot yet see which of its service lines (surgical orthopedics, sports-medicine visits, imaging, physical therapy) or which of its 8 locations are contribution-positive versus contribution-negative after fully loaded labor and overhead. This blind spot means the margin compression from 10% to 6% cannot be attributed to a specific payer, service, or site without further analysis.
